 Distance alone no ground to bypass Sessions Court for anticipatory bail: Rajasthan High Court
 Rajasthan High Court says living far from the Sessions Court is not enough for a direct anticipatory bail plea, and sends two accused to Udaipur.
 PCP Bureau Published: October 23, 2026, 9:23 am 
 Share Home » Rajasthan High Court » Raj HC Jodhpur » Distance alone no ground to bypass Sessions Court for anticipatory bail: Rajasthan High Court 
 The bench of Justice Sanjeet Purohit
 Jodhpur: The Rajasthan High Court has refused to hear anticipatory bail pleas filed directly before it by two accused from Chhattisgarh. It held that living far from the Sessions Court is not an extraordinary circumstance.
 Justice Sanjeet Purohit said Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita gives both courts concurrent jurisdiction. Even so, the Sessions Court should ordinarily be approached first. He dismissed the applications without giving any opinion on the merits of bail.
 The Court quoted the Supreme Court’s order in Mohammed Rasal C v State of Kerala : “… no person seeking such remedy should be encouraged or allowed to directly approach the High Court … by bypassing the jurisdiction of the concerned Sessions Court.”

The offences invoked include provisions of the BNS, the Rajasthan anti-conversion law and the SC/ST Atrocities Act.
 The applicants were not named in the FIR. They were added later on the statements of co-accused. One is a driver who worked for a co-accused, and the other is that co-accused’s wife. A charge sheet has been filed against the others, who were later granted bail by the Supreme Court. The investigation against the applicants is still pending.
 To justify coming directly to the High Court, the applicants pleaded four things. They live in Durg, Chhattisgarh, about 1,600 km from Udaipur. They faced imminent arrest. The co-accused’s bail pleas had earlier been rejected. And they feared for their safety and a fair hearing.
 The Court rejected each ground. It said their counsel could pursue the plea in Udaipur without their presence. Jodhpur is at a comparable distance from Durg, and they had engaged counsel here without any difficulty. It added that treating distance as enough would oust the Sessions Court in almost every case with an outstation accused.
 On the co-accused’s bail rejection, the Court said the applicants themselves argued that their roles were different. If this were enough, every co-accused would come straight to the High Court after the first one is refused bail below.
 The safety fear was found to rest on no specific material. On arrest, the Court noted that neither applicant had been arrested even though the charge sheet against the others was filed in September. One applicant was present in Court without any protection and was still not arrested.
 The Court also noted that the Supreme Court has reserved judgment in Mohammed Rasal C on this very question before a three-judge bench. It decided the plea on the present law because of the urgency pressed by the applicants.
 The Public Prosecutor argued that the SC/ST Act bars anticipatory bail. The applicants said they belong to notified Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe communities of Chhattisgarh, so the Act would not apply. The Investigating Officer said some material suggested they profess Christianity, but that the matter needed investigation. The Court left the question open for the competent court.
 The applicants can move the Sessions Court or the Special Court. That court has been asked to decide quickly and on its own merits, without being influenced by the High Court’s observations.
